entry.title: Machine reading and Spatial Geometry
entry.content:
In my last post on BPE Tokenizers, I discussed how machines break down words that they have never seen before. But knowing new words isn’t the same as using them in the right context. One possible way for machines to learn context is by calculating full-vocabulary probabilities across billions of words, but that would be a computational nightmare. So, researchers introduced Skip-Gram with Negative Sampling (SGNS) - a smart approach that learns word vectors by training a model to distinguish authentic word pairs from artificially generated “negative” ones.

Traditional language models work by taking a sequence of context words and then trying to predict the single next word. Skip-gram reverses this entire process. Instead of feeding the model a full sentence and asking it to guess the next word, Skip-gram is given a center word (target) and is asked to predict the surrounding neighbourhood of words (context window). Consider the example: “I want to have warm coffee this morning.” Here, “coffee” is the target word and we will be using a size 2 sliding window. Target: coffee Context: [“have”, “warm”, “this”, “morning”] The model creates training pairs directly from this window: (coffee, have) (coffee, warm) (coffee, this) (coffee, morning) Inverting the problem works because the model does not have to predict all of its surrounding neighbours at once. It evaluates each target-context pair independently, ignoring word order so that words that share similar neighbours naturally align in vector space.

When the model looks at a training pair like (coffee, warm), it computes the dot product of the vector “coffee” and the vector for “warm”. If the value of the dot product is high, then the vectors are pointing in the same direction in geometric space. If they are unrelated, the number is low. The raw dot product that we have now calculated isn’t probability. To calculate how confident the model is about “warm” compared to other words in the vocabulary, the model runs a formula called Softmax. To calculate the probability of “warm”, the model must take the exponential of its score and divide it by the sum of exponentials of all words in the entire dictionary (|V|): \(\text{Probability}(\text{"warm"} \mid \text{"coffee"}) = \frac{e^{\text{score}(\text{coffee, warm})}}{\sum_{w=1}^{|V|} e^{\text{score}(\text{coffee, } w)}}\) This is a major bottleneck because if my vocabulary has 1,000,000 words, then the model is required to calculate the exponentials of this huge denominator of all 1,000,000 words for every single pair. This would be computationally infeasible.

To bypass this challenge, researchers built a conceptual shortcut: Negative Sampling. Instead of asking the model “Out of 1,000,000 words in the vocabulary, which word is the correct neighbour?” negative sampling reframes the problem into a simple True vs. Fake Quiz. For every pair, instead of scoring the entire dictionary, the model has to only evaluate a few words. For example, Target: coffee | Neighbour: warm -> Label: TRUE(1) Target: coffee | Neighbour: tree -> Label: FAKE(0) Target: coffee | Neighbour: airport -> FAKE(0) Target: coffee | Neighbour: museum -> FAKE(0) Target: coffee | Neighbour: dog -> FAKE(0) Target: coffee | Neighbour: woman -> FAKE(0) Instead of updating a huge matrix across millions of classes for every single step, the model adjusts the weights slightly so that only the true neighbour (warm) gets high scores and the fake neighbours (tree, airport, museum, dog, woman) get low scores.

One important caveat is that the model does not pre-build a permanent list of words that can never go together. In daily conversations, almost any of the above words can come together in a sentence. For example, “I drank my coffee at the airport” has “airport” as a neighbour of “coffee”. Every time the model sees the training pair (coffee, warm), the training pipeline looks into the master dictionary and grabs 5 other words randomly. For that sentence, these 5 random words are assigned a label FAKE(0). However, in a later step, if any of those random words actually show up in a real sentence, then it gets labeled TRUE(1).

To summarize, Skip-gram with Negative Sampling (SGNS) gave machines a spatial map of how words relate in context without having to run through the entire vocabulary. While SGNS uses static vectors, modern LLMs use dynamic, contextual embeddings as soon as they see a sentence.

entry.title: How Technology Silences Low Resource Languages

link.title: How Technology Silences Low Resource Languages

entry.content:
I often wonder how people who speak high-resource languages have the best communication technologies by their side. The other day, I wanted to send holiday wishes to my friends and family in my native language, Kannada, but my keyboard kept converting my words into the wrong Kannada script, and Google Translate wasn’t any better. So, I ended up typing the same message in Kannada, but in English letters. The minute I transliterated my words, the emotion and excitement in my voice were instantly flattened. It felt like every other message that I send to anyone on any normal day.

Kannada is a morphologically complex language. A whole sentence in English can be merged into a single word in Kannada. It is a Dravidian language, a sibling of Tamil, with centuries of borrowing from Sanskrit. For languages like English, it is easy to break the words into suffixes and only understand the root word. This makes it easier to train models too and it’s also what makes low-resource languages which do not follow linguistic structures like English difficult for a model to learn and understand. When technology is built mainly for speakers of a few languages, it makes others unable to express their emotions and perspectives the right way.

The downstream effect of burying the voices of people is far more detrimental than just the inability to use technology. When people switch to English to express their opinions, there is less data online about these languages, leading to poor software tools and people being discouraged from using the language itself. Speaking in English also makes us lose the nuances, humor and phrases commonly used in the language. Progress has been very slow, and for everyday users like me, the tools still fall short.

Kannada is a language that has survived for centuries, only to feel invisible after a few years of English-first tech. Despite these challenges, I believe that Kannada will endure, not because technology will save it, but because the speakers keep choosing it.

ಸಿರಿಗನ್ನಡಂ ಗೆಲ್ಗೆ, ಸಿರಿಗನ್ನಡಂ ಬಾಳ್ಗೆ! (Translation: Long live rich Kannada! May rich Kannada triumph and thrive!)

entry.title: How LLMs Read: Byte Pair Encoding

link.title: How LLMs Read: Byte Pair Encoding

entry.content:
Imagine having to learn every single word and punctuation mark from a book. Now you’ll have to keep this in memory all your life. Later, you’re given one more book and another that you have to keep in memory. That would be difficult right? Now imagine trying to teach an LLM all these words. Even with all the compute in the world, an LLM might learn every single word from every text document on the planet. But what would happen once it comes across an error? If modern LLMs broke down every time it saw an error, we wouldn’t be where we are now. This is where subword tokenization finds the exact middle ground between memory efficiency and open-vocabulary expression. Byte-pair encodings do not understand the meaning of the word. They instead focus on breaking the word into individual characters with the end-of-word marker (.). For example, if a paragraph contains the word lower, this is how a machine would break it down: l o w e r. Now it looks at its trained list of merge rules - these rules are stored in the exact chronological order in which they were learned). It checks if any pair in the word match against the highest-priority rule:

Rule 1: l + o → lo
Result: lo w e r

Rule 2: lo + w → low
Result: low e r .

Rule 3: e + r → er
Result: er .

The word lower has now been successfully tokenized to ["low", "er"].

Even if the paragraph contains a new word, completely unseen by an LLM, it will use the same mechanics to break down the word. The tokenizer will not crash in this instance. Instead, it will keep chopping the words until the very last character to match the tokens in its vocabulary.

Earlier BPE focused only on alphabets. But what if a model encounters an emoji, non-English characters or code snippets with white spaces? The model would crash again. So, from GPT 2 onwards, companies started running BPE over raw bytes (0-255) over alphabets. This ensured that every single character could now be broken down into known tokens, eliminating the risk of unknown character errors.

BPE is a fundamental method used in all modern GenAI models. It offers real engineering trade-offs and better production realities. With vocabulary size as a hyperparameter, models can learn a small vocabulary which equates shorter training longer text sequences as opposed to a massive vocabulary that has shorter sequences and embedding matrices that can swallow GPU memory. Production tokenizers also require heavy optimization (like Rust implementations and pre-tokenization regex splits) so that preparing billions of tokens doesn’t stall the training pipelines.

entry.title: Reddit Lied To Me (Statistically Speaking)
entry.content:
It was a Friday night, I was all ready to snuggle in my bed when a random thought popped into my head. I badly wanted to know if I’d get into my favourite grad school. The thought got the better of me and I saw myself scrolling Reddit to find answers. I could see a sub called “r/gradadmissions” talk heavily about who got into which school and what their profile looked like. I thought this was the best place to look into to assuage my fears, if only best meant diving straight into panic mode. I went through around 10 posts that described how they got rejected from that school. One person posted that they had 2 top-tier publications and straight As, but they still got rejected. This was the end of me. I looked at more posts and every other post made me feel bitter. So I just turned off my phone and closed my eyes. All I could think of was how terrible this rejection would be for me. I was too stressed to sleep but it was now too late to call my friends for help. I realized there’s nothing I could do right away and managed to get some sleep.

I woke up in the morning with a dull ache in my chest. I knew I had to do something about this uncertainty. I called my friend and told her my fears. She told me to stop looking at Reddit because there’s a lot of “selection bias” in posts online, whatever that meant. She also told me that she had no publications but she got in, she also knew another girl who had poor grades got into an Ivy League PhD program. This conversation calmed me down and I felt pretty confident the next couple of days. Then I got curious.

I started looking into “selection bias”. Apparently, it means when what we see has been filtered in a way that makes it unrepresentative, so we draw conclusions about everyone from a slice that isn’t like everyone. Of course. Mostly anxious or rejected people would post on r/gradadmissions. The ones who got in would be celebrating. This made complete sense and I was so glad I caught onto it. But, along with selection bias, I also learned about “survivorship bias”. Survivorship bias is a type of selection bias where the filter is “only the successes remain visible.” Then it hit me. My friend’s stories were filtered too. There may be so many people who did not get in with no publications. Well, now I am back to square one. I thought I’d panic but somehow I remained peaceful. I understood that there were too many factors well beyond my control at play here. I haven’t found a solution for my problems yet, but I have learned to hold the tantrums my thoughts throw once in a while.

Moral of the story: Now, whenever I read something on the Internet, I ask myself who’s missing from this picture?
entry.summary: How a midnight scroll through r/gradadmissions taught me about survivorship bias.

entry.title: The Problem with Teaching AI what Hate Speech Means

link.title: The Problem with Teaching AI what Hate Speech Means

entry.content:
Cambridge defines hate speech as “public speech that expresses hate or encourages violence towards a person or group based on something such as race, religion, sex, or sexual orientation”. But Wikipedia notes that there is no single, consistent definition for hate speech. When a concept has no fixed definition, how do we define its boundaries? And when we as humans cannot define a concept, how can we teach it to AI? These were the exact questions I faced in my research.

Going through 2000+ toxic posts, I felt that all posts were hateful or malicious. It was so difficult to not label posts with slurs as not hateful. Then, I saw posts by members of the LGBTQ+ community using the word “queer”. Initially, I thought “queer” was a slur, but later realized that it was a reclaimed word that LGBTQ members now used. This questioned my entire basis for labeling posts as toxic or not. If the presence or absence of words by certain members of the community can make so much difference, I wanted to be careful about who gets heard on the Internet.

I was more careful now with my annotation strategies. I read multiple papers about hate speech and free speech to make sure I do not bury the voices that need to be heard the most. But I still failed at edge cases where I wasn’t sure if a post was hateful or not. Consider the example “These people are destroying our country.”. There are multiple ways of understanding this sentence - it can be political criticism, coded racism or just frustration. There is no way to understand the intention of the user through this sentence, even for a human being. An AI classifier is much further from understanding this context, which is what makes the task all the more nuanced.

Despite being cautious about annotation, my classifier still got it wrong in many contexts. The issue didn’t stop here. These erroneous labels went to my downstream application and there were many wrong labels. How can I trust an application that has learned false signals? Should I be worried about my voice being trampled because an AI couldn’t get a definition right? There are many papers that have tried tackling this challenge and many have come to the same conclusion of construct instability of community-specific concepts. This is also what has motivated me to work on reference-free frameworks which do not require a fixed definition or information about user demographics to build a trustworthy NLP measurement tool. Uncertainty quantification methods can also help LLMs surface labels that were labeled doubtfully. Going through those posts changed how I think about what we’re building. Every wrong label is a decision about whose voice gets heard. And I want to build systems that get this decision right.

entry.title: Cosine Similarity
entry.content:
In this post, we will be understanding the geometry of word embeddings. Word embeddings allow us to create a geometric landscape that shape the meaning based on where we are standing and in which direction. Earlier, one-hot encoding was used to obtain a vector representation of an array. For example, if we had an array A = [cat, dog, lion, elephant], then cat would be encoded as [1,0,0,0], dog as [0,1,0,0], lion as [0,0,1,0] and elephant as [0,0,0,1]. It is impossible to find the angle of similarity in this case because 0 multiplied with any number would give 0. So the similarity would be 0 no matter how probable the next word is. There would be no difference between the words ‘cat’ and ‘dog’ ,just like there would be no difference between ‘cat’ and ‘aeroplane’.

An embedding space on the other hand would be a vector of similarities, like [0.11, -.58, 0.67, 0.43]. It represents semantic traits along axes we don’t explicitly name. Words with similar meanings, like cat and dog, end up close to each other because they were found together in many texts.

The very first technique we think of when we hear measuring distance between two points is the Euclidean distance, i.e.,

\[d(u,v) = \|u - v\|_2 = \sqrt{\sum (u_i - v_i)^2}\]

Consider the sentence “The cat chased the mouse across the threshold of the kitchen, while the dog watched the scene from the porch of the house near the river.”. This sentence already contains 9 “the” words, but words like “cat”, “mouse”, “dog” appear just once. So, the algorithm would think that there is a high similarity between “the” and any other word. So the model ends up learning nothing useful. Let’s take a small example to illustrate this challenge:

“the” (A hyper-frequent filler word that appears everywhere):

\[v_{\text{the}} = [2.5, 3.0, 4.0]\]

“house” (A specific, content-heavy noun):

\[v_{\text{house}} = [0.5, 0.6, 0.8]\]

Let’s find the “length” (magnitude) of each word’s vector using the L2 norm formula ($\sqrt{\sum x^2}$):

  • Length of “the”: \(\|v_{\text{the}}\|_2 = \sqrt{2.5^2 + 3.0^2 + 4.0^2} = \sqrt{6.25 + 9.0 + 16.0} = \sqrt{31.25} \approx 5.59\)

  • Length of “house”: \(\|v_{\text{house}}\|_2 = \sqrt{0.5^2 + 0.6^2 + 0.8^2} = \sqrt{0.25 + 0.36 + 0.64} = \sqrt{1.25} \approx 1.12\)

Because of this huge value of “the”, the model will think that there is no relation between “house” and “the”. Cosine similarity, on the other hand, strips away the frequency-driven size of the vector and only looks at what direction the word is pointing.

Cosine similarity does not consider the magnitude and measures only the angle between two vectors.

\[\text{Sim}(u, v) = \frac{u \cdot v}{\|u\|_2 \|v\|_2}\]

If two vectors are unrelated, then the angle would be 90 degree. If they are exact opposites, it would be -1.0 and if they were related, it would be 1.0. By L2-normalizing every vector beforehand, the dot-product of two normalized vectors becomes their cosine similarity.

NumPy Implementation

import numpy as np

# 1. Mock 4-dimensional embeddings for a 5-word vocabulary
vocab = ["king", "man", "queen", "woman", "apple"]

E = np.array([
    [0.50, 0.70, 0.20, 0.90],  # king
    [0.40, 0.80, 0.10, 0.30],  # man
    [0.55, 0.25, 0.85, 0.95],  # queen
    [0.45, 0.35, 0.80, 0.35],  # woman
    [0.05, 0.10, 0.05, 0.05]   # apple
])

# 2. Matrix-wide L2 Normalization (keepdims=True ensures proper broadcasting)
norms = np.linalg.norm(E, axis=1, keepdims=True)
E_norm = E / norms

# 3. Pairwise Cosine Similarity Matrix (5x5) via single matrix multiplication
similarity_matrix = E_norm @ E_norm.T

print("Pairwise Similarity Matrix shape:", similarity_matrix.shape)
print(np.round(similarity_matrix, 2))

In this post, I have considered a toy example to illustrate the calculation of vectors of an array. In reality, before training, a word embedding model assigns a random vector to each word. The model is given a massive task to go through billions of text documents. Every time it sees the word “house”, it updates the vector. It does the same for “the” as well. However, since we are normalizing the vectors, the number of “the” in a sentence does not matter to the model.

entry.title: Demystifying Knowledge Distillation: Math, Gradients, and NumPy Implementations

link.title: Demystifying Knowledge Distillation: Math, Gradients, and NumPy Implementations

entry.content:
Knowledge distillation is a concept where a smaller “student” model learns from a larger, pre-trained “teacher” model. Instead of training the student on hard labels like [0,0,1], the student is trained to match the soft probabilities produced by the teacher model, like [0.067, 0.1345, 0.7985]. These soft targets contain “dark knowledge” – richer information about class similarities, such as a cat looking more like a dog than a car.

To generate soft probabilities, we take the raw outputs of the final layer of a neural network, called logits, and pass them through a temperature-scaled Softmax function. The temperature T controls how sharp or flat the probability distribution becomes. Standard softmax (T=1) produces highly confident “peaked” predictions, hiding the dark knowledge in near-zero probabilities. Raising T flattens the distribution and exposes the relative relationships across non-target classes so the student can learn more efficiently.

Temperature Scaling and Dark Knowledge

To implement temperature-scaled Softmax, we modify the standard Softmax formula by dividing the raw logits by T before exponentiating:

\[q_i = \frac{\exp(z_i / T)}{\sum_j \exp(z_j / T)}\]

In NumPy, we subtract the max logit for numerical stability:

import numpy as np

def softmax_with_temperature(logits: np.ndarray, T: float = 1.0) -> np.ndarray:
    scaled_logits = (logits - np.max(logits, axis=-1, keepdims=True)) / T
    exp_logits = np.exp(scaled_logits)
    return exp_logits / np.sum(exp_logits, axis=-1, keepdims=True)

To see temperature scaling in action, consider a teacher model outputting logits v = [10.0, 5.0, -2.0] for [Cat, Dog, Car]:

Temperature (T) Soft Probabilities Behavior
T = 1.0 [0.9933, 0.0067, 0.0000] Sharp: ~99.3% confident in Cat. Dog and Car are buried.
T = 2.0 [0.9168, 0.0753, 0.0079] Dog starts to show a signal over Car.
T = 5.0 [0.6033, 0.2220, 0.0544] Dog holds 22.2%, clearly a plausible second choice.
T = 20.0 [0.4228, 0.3326, 0.2446] Flat: Dog is much closer to Cat than Car is.

At high temperatures, the teacher reveals the structural landscape of the dataset – the precise dark knowledge the student needs to mimic.

Gradient Dynamics and the T² Scaling Factor

Once we obtain soft probability distributions p (teacher) and q (student), we measure how far apart they are using Soft Cross-Entropy. However, turning up temperature T introduces a subtle trap: it destroys the magnitude of our gradients during backpropagation.

The Vanishing Gradient Problem

The standard soft cross-entropy loss is:

\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{soft\_raw}} = -\sum_i p_i \log(q_i)\]

When we scale logits by T, applying the chain rule gives:

\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{soft\_raw}}}{\partial z} = \frac{1}{T}(q - p)\]

As T increases, two things happen simultaneously:

  1. The difference (q - p) shrinks because higher temperatures flatten both distributions.
  2. The entire expression is multiplied by 1/T.

Because (q - p) scales roughly as O(1/T), the gradient shrinks at O(1/T²). If you raise T to 20 or 100, your gradients vanish to near-zero and the student stops learning.

The Fix: Multiplying Loss by T²

Geoffrey Hinton et al. scaled the soft cross-entropy loss by T²:

\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{soft}} = -T^2 \sum_i p_i \log(q_i)\]

Taking the derivative, one factor of T cancels out:

\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{soft}}}{\partial z} = T^2 \cdot \frac{1}{T}(q - p) = T(q - p)\]

This T² multiplier restores scale invariance, keeping gradient magnitudes steady across different values of T.

Numerical Proof in NumPy

import numpy as np

def softmax_with_temp(logits: np.ndarray, T: float) -> np.ndarray:
    scaled = (logits - np.max(logits, axis=-1, keepdims=True)) / T
    exp_logits = np.exp(scaled)
    return exp_logits / np.sum(exp_logits, axis=-1, keepdims=True)

v = np.array([2.0, 5.0, 1.0])
z = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 0.0])

print(f"{'Temp (T)':<10} | {'Unscaled Grad (q - p)/T':<25} | {'Scaled Grad T * (q - p)':<25}")
print("-" * 65)

for T in [1.0, 5.0, 20.0, 100.0]:
    p = softmax_with_temp(v, T)
    q = softmax_with_temp(z, T)
    grad_unscaled = (q - p) / T
    grad_scaled = T * (q - p)
    print(f"T = {T:<8} | {str(np.round(grad_unscaled, 5)):<25} | {str(np.round(grad_scaled, 4)):<25}")

Output:

Temp (T)   | Unscaled Grad (q - p)/T    | Scaled Grad T * (q - p)
-----------------------------------------------------------------
T = 1.0    | [ 0.19812 -0.271    0.07288] | [ 0.1981 -0.271   0.0729]
T = 5.0    | [ 0.01085 -0.01974  0.00889] | [ 0.2714 -0.4935  0.2222]
T = 20.0   | [ 0.00059 -0.00115  0.00056] | [ 0.2366 -0.4616  0.225 ]
T = 100.0  | [ 0.00002 -0.00004  0.00002] | [ 0.2252 -0.4481  0.2229]

Without T² scaling, the gradient collapses from 0.1981 down to 0.00002 as T increases. With T² scaling, the gradient stabilizes around [0.225, -0.448, 0.222] regardless of temperature.

These soft targets contain “dark knowledge” – richer information about class similarities, such as a cat looking more like a dog than a car.

entry.title: The Party Whisper
entry.content:
Sherry was invited to a party by her close friend she knew from childhood, Nicole. They had grown together in the same town and went to the same university. Nicole loved having friends over, but this time around the party was huge. Sherry guessed at least two hundred. She arrived at 7 P.M. sharp, greeted Nicole and her husband and made herself comfortable at a table with other friends of the host. There was a lot of smiling, laughing and introducing one another.

Everyone at the table was involved in a deep discussion on makeup trends when Sarah pulled Erica to a corner. Sherry was watching the two and Erica sounded surprised. She gasped and kept sighing. “Wonder what that was,” thought Sherry. Anyhow, she was never one to gossip so she never bothered asking anyone.

A couple of minutes later, Sherry saw Erica whispering something to Carol. Carol was also shocked and flabbergasted. This went on and on until at least ten other people were involved in this little whispered secret. Miranda was the last to receive it and, much to everyone’s surprise, she went ahead and whispered it back into Sarah’s ears.

The reaction, however, was much different this time. Sarah was angry and was yelling at Erica and Miranda. The whole party saw the fight play out. Apparently, Sarah had said that Grace had got a promotion and was moving to Paris. But Miranda received the message as Grace was leaving her husband and was planning to elope with a French man. Grace, who was also at the party, started sobbing. Poor Grace – there was no fault of hers. Sarah was embarrassed, but she had no way to figure out who had twisted her message.

Alas, there is no way to control gossip.

Note: This story is entirely my own. The idea, the characters, and the writing was all mine. No AI was used in any part of this post. All grammar mistakes and errors are mine.

entry.title: Economic Shocks and Online Extremism: A Difference-in-Differences Approach

link.title: Economic Shocks and Online Extremism: A Difference-in-Differences Approach

entry.content:
Online extremism mostly relies on blaming an out-group community like women, members of the LGBTQ community, immigrants, or minorities. When an external event occurs, it is important to understand how communities respond, as it can lead to an increase or decrease in scapegoating. This post explores how we can study online extremism and economic scapegoating using a difference-in-differences design.

Difference-in-differences is a type of event study used to detect changes in behavior of a group after an event stimulus. In my research, I considered two ideologically distinct types of communities: political and apolitical forums. The political forums, including Stormfront, Vanguard, and White Nations, discuss immigration, minorities, and political grievances directed at out-group communities. The apolitical forums, including pickup artist forums, Men Going Their Own Way (MGTOW), and Incelsis, focus on relationships with women. Both types of forums have different triggers. When a positive job surprise occurred, the two communities reacted very differently. Politically charged forums showed a reduction in economic grievance posting, suggesting less scapegoating when economic conditions improve. Apolitical forums showed no significant change. Notably, before the event, both forum types recorded similar levels of economic grievance posts, a finding confirmed by pre-trend analysis, which validates that the difference-in-differences design is appropriate here.

This analysis reveals that in-group communities use external events to scapegoat out-group communities whenever their group does not personally benefit from a change. This distinction is important because it exposes the real motive behind extremist community behavior.

With this finding in mind, policymakers can better understand why extremist communities proliferate and how monitoring out-group blame patterns could help identify when communities are most likely to escalate.

Note: This post was written by me. AI was used for minor grammar and phrasing suggestions only.
entry.summary: Online extremism mostly relies on blaming an out-group community like women, members of the LGBTQ community, immigrants, or minorities. When an external event occurs, it is important to understand how communities respond, as it can lead to an increase or decrease in scapegoating. This post explores how we can study online extremism and economic scapegoating using a difference-in-differences design.

entry.title: Bias-Variance Tradeoff
entry.content:
In today’s post, I’ll be discussing bias-variance trade-off, lesser in technical depth, but more towards simple understanding about the topic at hand. As and when I write more blogs, I intend to make them more technical. Bias in machine learning is the inability of a machine learning method to capture the true relationship between variables and target.

The straight line in the first image shows high bias i.e., the error between actual and predicted values on the testing set is high. Whereas in the squiggly line in the second image, the same error is very low, meaning low bias.

Variance is the difference in fits between different data sets.

The straight line in the first image shows low variance i.e., the error between actual and predicted values on the testing set is comparatively low. Whereas in the squiggly line in the second image, the same error in very high, meaning high variance. Ideally, we would prefer a machine learning model that has low bias and low variance, but practical models don’t behave that way. There are several methods like regularization, bagging and boosting to obtain the ‘sweet spot’ between the two extremes of bias and variance. Because the squiggly line fits the training set perfectly, but performs poorly on the testing set, we say that the second image is overfit. When the model doesn’t fit the testing set well, then the model is said to be underfitting. We can use the formula below to check if the model is overfitting (high variance) or if we need to use more complex models: Err(x₀) = E[(Y − f̂(x₀))² | X = x₀] = σ²ε (Irreducible error) +[E f̂(x₀) − f(x₀)]² (Bias2) + E[f̂(x₀) − E f̂(x₀)]² (Variance) Err(x₀) = E[(Y − f̂(x₀))² | X = x₀] = expected prediction error at point x₀ i.e., how wrong is our model on average at this point. σ²ε (Irreducible error) = noise in the data itself, no matter how good the model is, more like randomness in the real world. [E f̂(x₀) − f(x₀)]² (Bias2) = how far our average prediction is from truth. E[f̂(x₀) − E f̂(x₀)]² (Variance) = how much do our predictions fluctuate across different training sets. References:

  1. StatQuest (2018). Bias and Variance. YouTube. https://youtu.be/EuBBz3bI-aA?si=bOGTF8ejnq86YWsM
  2. Hastie, T., Tibshirani, R., & Friedman, J. (2009). The Elements of Statistical Learning.

On AI use: This content has been written entirely by me. This includes ideation, writing and fact-checking. I haven’t used AI to polish the sentences/check for spelling or grammar mistakes. The images in this post have been generated with the help of Gemini.
entry.summary: A beginner-friendly introduction to bias-variance tradeoff in machine learning.
